entry:
Event celebrated by a community and centered on one or more characteristic aspects of its religion, traditions, or cultures. Festivals are often observed as indigenous or national holidays, religious celebrations, or cultural fairs (*mela*). Besides religion and [[Folklore|folklore]], a significant source has been [[Agriculture|agriculture]]: many festivals are associated with harvest time, and thanksgiving for good harvests is integrated into autumn celebrations such as [[Halloween]] in the Northern Hemisphere and [[Easter]] in the Southern Hemisphere.

Festivals often serve communal purposes, especially commemorating or giving thanks to gods, goddesses, or saints; these are called patronal festivals. They also provide entertainment, which was particularly important to local communities before mass-produced entertainment, and those focused on cultural or ethnic topics inform members of their traditions.

The word was first used as an adjective in the late 14th century, via Old French from Latin; its first recorded use as a noun was in 1589. Festivals are found in virtually all cultures, and Saturnalia was likely influential on [[Christmas]] and Carnival. The Avignon Festival and the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, both established in 1947, were influential in shaping the modern festival model.

The most important religious festivals, such as Christmas, Rosh Hashanah, [[Diwali]], Holi, Eid al-Fitr, and Eid al-Adha, mark out the year. Historical events such as military victories also prompt festivals; an early example was established by the pharaoh [[Ramesses III]] to celebrate his victory over the Libyans. [[Passover]] and Easter are moveable feasts, determined by lunar or agricultural cycles or the calendar in use. The vast majority of festivals are local and modest.

Creative work, chiefly narrative, portraying individuals, events, or places that are imaginary or in ways that are imaginary. Fictional portrayals are thus inconsistent with fact, history, or plausibility. In a traditional narrow sense, fiction refers to written narratives in prose, often specifically [[Novel|novels]], novellas, and short stories. More broadly, it encompasses imaginary narratives in any medium, including theatrical performances, films, television programs, comics, role-playing games, and video games.

The fictionality of a work is typically expressed publicly, so audiences expect it to deviate to some degree from the real world. Some works depict an independent [[Fictional universe|fictional universe]]; constructing one is called worldbuilding. The study of the nature, function, and meaning of fiction is literary theory, and the interpretation of specific texts is [[Literary criticism]]. The critic James Wood argues that "fiction is both artifice and verisimilitude," a requirement often linked to Samuel Taylor Coleridge's idea of the audience's willing suspension of disbelief.

Fiction contrasts with [[Non-fiction|non-fiction]], whose creators assume responsibility for presenting only historical and factual reality, although works such as autofiction and docudramas blur the boundary. Speculative fiction adheres less to realistic or plausible individuals, events, or places and includes fantasy, alternative history, and [[Science fiction]]. Realistic fiction has a real setting and believable events; its subgenres include [[Historical fiction]].

Early fiction was closely associated with history and myth. Greek poets such as [[Homer]], Hesiod, and Aesop developed fictional stories told first orally and then in writing, and prose fiction developed in [[Ancient Greece]]. Plato condemned fiction as thrice-removed imitation that deceives, while modern analyses frame it as non-deceptive pretense.

Work of visual art that simulates experiences and communicates ideas, stories, perceptions, emotions, or atmosphere through moving images, generally synchronized with sound since the 1930s; also called a movie or motion picture. Films are produced by recording people and objects with cameras or by creating them using [[Animation|animation]] techniques and [[Special effect|special effects]]. They comprise a series of individual frames which, shown rapidly in succession, create the illusion of motion; flickering between frames is not noticeable because of an effect now called flicker fusion.

Films are widely considered an important art form: they entertain, educate, enlighten, and inspire audiences. Their visual elements need no translation, and with dubbing or subtitles any film can become a worldwide attraction. Films are also artifacts of specific cultures, which they reflect and in turn affect.

Film drew on earlier traditions including oral storytelling, literature, theater, and the visual arts, and on forms featuring projected images, such as shadow puppetry, the [[Camera obscura|camera obscura]], and the magic lantern. The stroboscopic animation principle was introduced in 1833 with the phénakisticope and later applied in the zoetrope (1866), the flip book (1868), and the praxinoscope (1877). [[Photography]] was introduced in 1839, but early emulsions needed exposures too long to record moving subjects. In 1878, [[Eadweard Muybridge]] photographed a running horse with a battery of cameras along a track and published the results as *The Horse in Motion*. In 1886, Ottomar Anschütz developed the Electrotachyscope, which displayed short loops of 24 glass plate photographs; some 152 coin-operated examples were manufactured in [[Berlin]] from 1891. Émile Reynaud's Théâtre Optique, patented in 1888, could project longer sequences with separate backgrounds.

Management, movement, investment, and raising of money; also the academic discipline that studies these. Based on scope, it divides into three primary branches: personal, corporate, and public finance. In the financial system, assets are bought, sold, or traded as financial instruments such as currencies, loans, [[Bond (finance)|bonds]], shares, options, futures, and swaps, and can also be banked, invested, and insured to maximize value and minimize loss. Risks are always present, and financial markets and institutions underpin the system.

Finance channels money from savers and investors to entities that need it. An entity whose income exceeds its expenditure can lend or invest the surplus; one whose income is less can raise capital by borrowing, by selling government or corporate bonds, or, for a corporation, by selling equity (stock or shares). Lending is often indirect, through an intermediary such as a [[Bank|bank]], which accepts deposits, pays interest, and lends to borrowers, earning the difference. Investment banks find initial investors and facilitate the listing of securities, and securities exchanges allow their trade thereafter. Large-scale inter-institutional trade is called wholesale finance; its mathematical "financial engineering" employs quantitative analysts.

Personal finance is budgeting to meet basic needs while keeping the risk of losing capital reasonable; it may involve education costs, financing real estate and cars, buying [[Insurance|insurance]], investing, and saving for retirement. Corporate finance concerns how firms raise capital and invest in projects, and public finance concerns government revenue, expenditure, and debt.

The early history of finance parallels that of [[Money|money]], which is prehistoric; ancient and medieval civilizations incorporated banking, trading, and accounting, and the global financial system formed in the late 19th century. The earliest doctoral programs in finance were established in the 1960s and 1970s. The field is related to [[Economics]] and business administration.

Rapid oxidation of a fuel in the exothermic chemical process of [[Combustion|combustion]], releasing heat, light, and various reaction products. Flames, the most visible portion of a fire, are produced when the fuel reaches its ignition point temperature. Flames from hydrocarbon fuels consist primarily of carbon dioxide, water vapor, oxygen, and nitrogen; if hot enough, the gases may become ionized to produce [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]]. The color and intensity of a flame depend on the fuel and the surrounding gases. Fire is sustained by four interdependent components: fuel, heat, oxygen, and a self-perpetuating chemical chain reaction, modeled as the fire tetrahedron; removing any one extinguishes it.

Fire directly affects land-based ecological systems worldwide. Its benefits include stimulating plant growth and maintaining ecological balance; its harms include hazards to life and property, atmospheric pollution, and water contamination. Burning vegetation releases nitrogen into the atmosphere, whereas potassium and phosphorus remain in the ash and are quickly recycled into the soil; the resulting loss of nitrogen produces a long-term reduction in soil fertility, which nitrogen-fixing plants such as clover, peas, and beans can help recover.

The fossil record of fire first appears with land-based flora in the Middle Ordovician, 470 million years ago. [[Wildfire]] became possible once atmospheric oxygen rose above 13%, and is first recorded in the Late Silurian, 420 million years ago, by fossils of charred plants. Fire became more abundant when grasses became dominant in many ecosystems, around 6 to 7 million years ago.

Control of fire was a dramatic change in the habits of early humans. It allowed cooking, which increased the variety and availability of nutrients and reduced disease by killing pathogens; provided warmth, allowing people to live in cooler climates; and kept nocturnal predators at bay. Evidence of occasional cooked food dates from 1 million years ago, and the oldest clear evidence of deliberate firemaking dates to around 400,000 years ago at Barnfield, England, where pyrite appears to have been struck against flint. Evidence becomes widespread around 50 to 100 thousand years ago. By the [[Neolithic Revolution]], people worldwide used fire in landscape management, including controlled burns and slash-and-burn agriculture, which remains common across much of tropical Africa, Asia, and South America. Globally, as much as 5 million sq km burns in a given year.

Fire has been used for cooking, heating, lighting, clearing land, signaling, propulsion, smelting, forging, waste incineration, cremation, rituals, and warfare, and was one of the four classical elements. In 1667 Johann Joachim Becher, and more formally in 1697 Georg Ernst Stahl, incorporated van Helmont's finding that burning charcoal released a gas into phlogiston theory. [[Antoine Lavoisier]] demonstrated that combustion did not involve the release of a substance but rather that something was being taken up. Most home fires start from unattended cooking, although cigarettes are another major cause; smoke detectors and sprinkler systems greatly reduce harm.

Gun that shoots projectiles using the explosive pressure generated by combustion (deflagration) of a chemical propellant, most often black powder in antique firearms and smokeless powder in modern ones. The term is defined variably, both technically and legally, in different countries. Small arms are the subset of light firearms designed to be readily carried and operated by an individual; they include handguns such as pistols, revolvers, and derringers, and long guns such as [[Rifle|rifles]], shotguns, submachine guns, and light machine guns.

The first firearms originated in 10th-century Song dynasty China, where bamboo tubes containing [[Gunpowder|gunpowder]] and pellet projectiles were mounted on spears to make the portable fire lance, which was used effectively as a shock weapon in the siege of De'an in 1132. In the 13th century, fire lance barrels were replaced with metal tubes and became the hand cannon, and the technology gradually spread throughout Eurasia during the 14th century. Beginning in the 1860s, black powder was gradually replaced by smokeless powder, which is mostly based on nitrocellulose. Most modern firearms, with the exception of smoothbore shotguns, have rifled barrels that impart a stabilizing spin to the bullet.

Modern firearms are described by caliber (bore diameter), by type of action (single-shot or repeating, such as bolt, lever, pump, revolver, semi-automatic, or fully automatic), by firing mechanism (such as matchlock, flintlock, or centerfire), and by intended use. The effective range of handguns and shotguns generally does not exceed 100 m, while most rifles are accurate to 500 m using iron sights, and sniper rifles to more than 2,000 m.

In the 2018 estimate of the Small Arms Survey, there were over one billion firearms worldwide, of which 857 million were in civilian hands; U.S. civilians accounted for 393 million. Firearm regulation remains the subject of ongoing public debate.

Aquatic, anamniotic, gill-bearing vertebrates with a tough cranium protecting the brain. Many have fins used for directional stability and propulsion. Fish are grouped into the more basal jawless fish and the more common jawed fish, which include all living cartilaginous and bony fish and the extinct placoderms and acanthodians. Because tetrapods are descended from fish, modern phylogenetics treats fish as a paraphyletic group that includes all vertebrates except tetrapods, and the class Pisces of older reference works is no longer used. The plural is *fish* for individuals and *fishes* for species.

Most fish are cold-blooded, though large, active swimmers such as the white shark and tuna can maintain a higher core temperature. Many communicate acoustically. The study of fish is ichthyology. There are over 33,000 extant species, more than all other traditional vertebrate classes combined. Most belong to the class [[Actinopterygii]], the ray-finned fishes, and about 96% of living species are teleosts, a crown group that can protrude their jaws.

About 530 million years ago, during the [[Cambrian explosion]], fishlike animals with a notochord, such as *Haikouichthys*, appear in the fossil record. The ostracoderms, the earliest fish with dedicated respiratory gills and paired fins, had heavy bony plates as protection against invertebrate predators. The first jawed fish, the [[Placoderm|placoderms]], appeared in the Silurian and diversified greatly during the Devonian, the "Age of Fishes." Bony fish, distinguished by swim bladders and later ossified endoskeletons, became dominant after the end-Devonian extinction wiped out the placoderms. [[Tetrapod|Tetrapods]] evolved from lobe-finned fish during the Carboniferous, developing air-breathing lungs homologous to swim bladders.

Fish have been an important natural resource for humans since prehistoric times, especially as food. They are harvested from wild fisheries or farmed, caught for recreation, and kept in aquaria. In human culture they have served as deities, religious symbols, and subjects of art, books, and films.

Activity of trying to catch fish. Fish are often caught from freshwater or marine environments, but may also be caught from stocked bodies of water such as ponds, canals, and reservoirs. Techniques include trawling, longlining, jigging, hand-gathering, spearing, netting, [[Angling|angling]], shooting, and trapping, as well as more destructive and often illegal methods such as electrocution, blasting, and poisoning. The term also covers catching crustaceans, shellfish, cephalopods, and echinoderms, but is not normally applied to harvesting farmed fish ([[Aquaculture|aquaculture]]) or to hunting aquatic mammals, for which terms such as [[Whaling|whaling]] are used.

Fishing dates back to at least the beginning of the Upper Paleolithic, about 40,000 years ago; isotopic analysis shows that Tianyuan man, a 40,000-year-old modern human from eastern Asia, regularly consumed freshwater fish. It is one of the few food production activities that persisted from prehistory into the modern age, surviving both the [[Neolithic Revolution]] and the Industrial Revolutions. Early permanent settlements such as Lepenski Vir are almost always associated with fishing as a major food source.

The modern fishing trawler was developed in the 19th century at the English port of Brixham, whose sleek, gaff-rigged trawlers were fast enough for long-distance trips and robust enough to tow large trawls in deep water. Grimsby grew to become the largest fishing port in the world by the mid-19th century, and its Royal Dock was opened by [[Queen Victoria]] in 1854. By the end of the 19th century, over 3,000 trawlers were in commission in Britain. The earliest steam-powered fishing boats appeared in the 1870s, and in 1877 David Allen built the first screw-propelled steam trawler in the world.

According to United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization statistics, there are an estimated 36.0 million commercial fishers and fish farmers, and fishing and aquaculture provide direct and indirect employment to over 500 million people in developing countries. In 2005, worldwide per capita consumption of wild-caught fish was 14.4 kg. Overexploitation, bycatch, and habitat disruption from bottom trawling are major concerns.

Overflow of water (rarely other fluids) that submerges land that is usually dry. Floods are of significant concern in agriculture, civil engineering, and public health, and are studied in [[Hydrology|hydrology]] and hydraulic engineering. Natural types include river flooding, groundwater flooding, coastal flooding, and urban flooding, sometimes known as [[Flash flood|flash flooding]]. Land may also be flooded intentionally for agricultural, military, or river-management purposes, as when paddy fields are prepared for rice.

Flooding may occur when a river, lake, sea, or ocean overtops or breaks [[Levee|levees]], or when rainwater accumulates on saturated ground, called an areal flood. Rivers flood when the flow rate exceeds the capacity of the channel, particularly at bends or meanders. Slow-rising floods most commonly occur in large rivers with large catchment areas and may result from sustained rainfall, rapid snowmelt, monsoons, or tropical cyclones. In the extremely flat Red River Valley of Minnesota, North Dakota, and Manitoba, where the river drops only 72 m over 890 km, a hybrid of river and areal flooding known locally as "overland flooding" can occur.

Human changes to the environment, such as [[Deforestation|deforestation]], removal of wetlands, changes in waterway course, and flood controls such as levees, often increase the intensity and frequency of flooding. [[Climate change]], through an intensified water cycle and sea level rise, is also cited as increasing flood risk, while natural variability in precipitation remains a major driver. Many people live and work near rivers because the land is flat and fertile and rivers provide travel and commerce, so floods often damage buildings on natural [[Floodplain|floodplains]].

Secondary impacts include a short-term increase in waterborne and vector-borne diseases and long-term displacement of residents. From 1990 to 2022, floods affected more than 3.2 billion people, caused 218,353 deaths, and caused more than 1.3 trillion USD in economic losses. Notable events include the [[1931 China floods]] and [[Hurricane Katrina]].

English social reformer, statistician, and founder of modern nursing. Born in Florence, Italy, to a wealthy British family, she was named after her birthplace. At sixteen she experienced what she later described as the first of several calls from God to service, and she rejected the expected role of wife and mother despite her family's opposition. After a nine-year courtship she rejected the politician and poet Richard Monckton Milnes, convinced that marriage would interfere with her calling. In Rome in 1847 she met Sidney Herbert, a politician who became a lifelong friend and later facilitated her work in the Crimea.

Nightingale came to prominence as a manager and trainer of nurses during the [[Crimean War]], in which she organized care for wounded soldiers at [[Constantinople]]. She significantly reduced death rates by improving [[Hygiene|hygiene]] and living standards, and became an icon of Victorian culture as "The Lady with the Lamp," making ward rounds at night. Some commentators have asserted that the media exaggerated her wartime achievements, but critics agree on the importance of her later work in professionalizing nursing for women.

In 1860 she established her nursing school at St Thomas' Hospital in London, the first secular nursing school in the world, now part of King's College London. She wrote *Notes on Nursing* (1859). The Nightingale Pledge, taken by new nurses, and the Florence Nightingale Medal, the highest international distinction a nurse can achieve, are named in her honor, and International Nurses Day is celebrated on her birthday.

She was also an innovator in [[Statistics|statistics]], presenting analyses in graphical form. She is famous for the polar area diagram, or Nightingale rose diagram, equivalent to a modern circular histogram. Her social reforms included improving healthcare for all sections of British society, advocating better hunger relief in [[India]], and helping to abolish prostitution laws that were harsh for women.
